author: Stanley Milgram
biz: Put the stop in the script, not the objection

Milgram's binding factor is sequence, and a phone or WhatsApp journey at HomeownersLoan is a sequence. This week, go through the adviser scripts and strip out every prod shaped rebuttal that exists only to keep a reluctant customer moving. Replace them with one written, authorised line that lets an adviser end a case on suitability grounds, and tell the team plainly that using it is a good outcome. Measure the number of enquiries closed by advisers as unsuitable each week, and track it alongside complaints and lapse rates rather than against conversion alone.
Make the pause the default for distressed callers

Debt Support Direct clients are often frightened, and a frightened person complies with whoever sounds official. That is exactly the dynamic Milgram measured, and it is the Consumer Duty risk too. This week, build a required pause into the call, where the adviser says the decision can wait, invites them to talk to someone they trust and offers to ring back. Then measure two things, the share of vulnerable clients who take at least a day before committing, and a short understanding check on what they think they have agreed to.
book: Obedience to Authority: An Experimental View

b: Stanley Milgram was born in the Bronx on the fifteenth of August 1933, the second of three children. His father Samuel was a baker who had come from Hungary. His mother Adele had come from Romania. Both had crossed to America around the time of the First World War, and the family lived by the business of bread, which means it lived by very early mornings and very thin margins.

Through his childhood the news from Europe got steadily worse, and then it arrived in person. Relatives who had survived the camps came to New York and stayed with the family for a time. At his bar mitzvah in 1946, aged thirteen, the boy stood up and spoke not about himself but about the plight of the Jews of Europe.

He never quite got over the accident of his own safety. In a letter written in 1958 he said that he should have been born into the German speaking Jewish community of Prague in 1922, and added that how he came to be born in the Bronx Hospital he would never quite understand.

That is the question underneath everything he later built. Not why monsters do terrible things. Monsters are easy. The question was why clerks and bakers and salesmen do them, and whether the men who had sheltered in his parents' flat had simply been unlucky in their neighbours.

b: He took his first degree in political science at Queens College in 1954, having never sat a single course in psychology. When he applied to Harvard to study social relations, they turned him down for exactly that reason. He was told he might reapply, talked his way in as a special student that autumn, did well, and was admitted as a proper student the following year.

His teacher there was Gordon Allport, who admired what he called the young man's limitless drive and persistence. While finishing his doctorate, Milgram worked as an assistant to Solomon Asch at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.

Asch had done the experiment everybody now half remembers. Show a person three lines of obviously different lengths, surround him with strangers who calmly name the wrong one, and a good proportion of people will name the wrong one too. Milgram thought the apparatus was brilliant and the subject matter thin. Lines do not matter.

He also saw a distinction that became the spine of his later work. Asch had studied conformity, which is sideways pressure from equals. What Milgram wanted was the vertical version. Conformity is imitation, and people deny it afterwards. Obedience is compliance with someone who has the right to ask, and people do not deny it at all. They point at the person who told them.

b: For his doctorate he rebuilt Asch's experiment for the ear and took it abroad. Instead of judging lines, his subjects sat with headphones and said which of two tones had lasted longer. The five other subjects pressing wrong answers around them were not people at all. They were tape recordings.

He ran nearly four hundred people through it in Norway and then in France, and reported that the Norwegians conformed more readily than the French. The finding is the least important part. What matters is the joke he made about his own invention, that the group is always willing to perform in the laboratory at the experimenter's convenience.

That sentence is the clue to the whole career. Milgram's real gift was not theory. It was apparatus. He could build a small sealed world in which something that is normally invisible, and that people will lie about if you simply ask them, becomes a number you can read off a dial.
He took his doctorate in 1960 and went straight to Yale as an assistant professor, carrying one unbuilt machine in his head.

b: The trial of Adolf Eichmann opened in Jerusalem in April 1961. About three months later, in the basement of Linsly Chittenden Hall at Yale, Milgram started running the experiment that would define him.

He advertised in the local paper for men to take part in a study of memory and learning, offering four dollars and fifty cents, and told them the money was theirs whatever happened once they arrived. Forty men came, aged twenty to fifty, from New Haven and the towns around it. Postal clerks, high school teachers, salesmen, engineers, labourers.

Two of the three people in the room were acting. The experimenter was a thirty one year old high school biology teacher, impassive and a little stern, in a grey technician's coat. The learner was a forty seven year old accountant of Irish American descent whom almost everybody found mild and likeable. The slips of paper that decided roles were rigged, so the real volunteer was always the teacher.

The teacher was given a sample shock so he knew what he was handing out. Then he was sat in front of a machine with thirty switches running from fifteen volts to four hundred and fifty, labelled in groups from slight shock up to danger severe shock, with the last two switches marked only with crosses. When the learner answered wrongly, the teacher moved one switch along.

If the teacher wanted to stop, the man in the coat had four lines, in order. Please continue, or please go on. The experiment requires that you continue. It is absolutely essential that you continue. You have no other choice, you must go on. And if the teacher asked whether the learner could be permanently injured, there was a fifth. Although the shocks may be painful, there is no permanent tissue damage, so please go on.
Nothing in that room was real except the pressure.

b: Before he ran it, Milgram asked psychiatrists, students and ordinary adults how far they thought people would go. The answers clustered around almost nobody. A pathological fringe, perhaps one person in a hundred, would reach the end of the board.

In the version he published first, the learner was out of sight and made no sound at all. At three hundred volts he pounded on the wall. After that there was nothing from the other room, which meant the teacher was now punishing a silence.

Twenty six of the forty men pushed every switch to the end. Fourteen broke off, five of them at the moment the pounding started and the rest in the handful of switches after it. Milgram wrote that subjects were observed to sweat, tremble, stutter, bite their lips, groan and dig their fingernails into their flesh. Fourteen of the forty laughed nervously, which he described as entirely out of place, even bizarre. One man, at the point of refusing, muttered, oh God, let's stop it.

The paper appeared in 1963. That autumn a headline in the New York Times told readers that sixty five percent in a test blindly obeyed an order to inflict pain, and the number has been doing the rounds ever since.

So had the row. A St Louis newspaper attacked Yale and Milgram over how the volunteers had been treated. Diana Baumrind argued in 1964 that he should have stopped the moment people were visibly in distress. The American Psychological Association held up his membership for a year before granting it in full, and in the same year the American Association for the Advancement of Science gave him its prize for behavioural research. He was thirty one and permanently famous for one thing.

b: The number everybody remembers is the least interesting thing he did. Over 1961 and 1962 he ran condition after condition, nearly a thousand people in all, altering one feature at a time and watching what the obedience rate did. The book is really a report on that machine of comparisons.

Distance was the first dial. Give the learner a voice, protesting and complaining of his heart, and obedience sat around sixty two in a hundred. Put him in the same room as the teacher and it fell to forty. Make the teacher hold the learner's hand down on the plate himself and it fell to thirty.

Authority was the second. When the experimenter left the room and gave his orders by telephone, obedience dropped to about one in five, and some men quietly pressed the lowest switch every time while assuring him they were following the schedule. When the whole study moved to an ordinary office in Bridgeport with no university name on the door, it only slipped to about forty eight in a hundred. The lab coat mattered more than the ivy.

The social dials were the sharpest of all. Put two other teachers in the room who refuse and walk out, and nine in ten real subjects refuse too. Give the subject a small subsidiary job while another man presses the lever, and more than nine in ten go all the way to the end. Let an ordinary man rather than the experimenter give the orders and obedience falls to about one in five. Women obeyed at the same rate as men and reported more strain doing it.

He also killed the comfortable explanation. When subjects were told to choose any shock level they liked, the average choice was under four switches out of thirty. They did not want to hurt anybody. The appetite was never the problem. The architecture was.

b: In the autumn of 1963 he went back to Harvard as an assistant professor on a three year contract. It was extended by one more year at the lower rank of lecturer, and then it ended. He was never given tenure. Colleagues were uneasy about him, and what they were uneasy about was the experiment. He found leaving very painful.
In 1967 the City University of New York made him a full professor outright, skipping the rank in between, to lead its social psychology programme. He stayed there for the rest of his life.

And he kept inventing apparatus. He posted bundles to a hundred and sixty people in Omaha and asked them to move each one, by hand, towards a stockbroker near Boston. The chains that arrived had run through between two and ten people, with a median of five, which is how the world acquired the phrase six degrees of separation. He published it in the first issue of Psychology Today in May 1967.

He scattered stamped addressed letters in the street to see which ones strangers would post on, and found that a letter to a likeable addressee came back far more often than a letter to a group people despised. He wrote about the experience of living in cities. He made films, and wrote poems, and was by all accounts much more interesting than his one famous result.

b: The book came out in 1974, thirteen years after the basement, and it is where he finally says what he thinks the dials mean. His central idea is the agentic state. A person who enters a hierarchy stops seeing himself as the author of his own acts and starts seeing himself as the instrument of someone else's purpose.

The important move is what happens to conscience. It does not switch off. It changes job. It stops asking whether the thing being done is right and starts asking whether it is being done well, so that a man can feel genuinely guilty about mispronouncing a word pair while delivering what he believes is a dangerous shock. Responsibility is handed upwards to whoever is thought to own the purpose.

He then explains why people stay in, which he calls binding factors. The act is sequential, so every switch is only slightly worse than the one just agreed to. The etiquette of the situation makes it rude to break your word and embarrass a man who has been nothing but polite. And disobedience carries an old learned anxiety that goes back further than any of us can remember.

Against that he sets strain, which builds as the victim suffers, and the little mechanisms people use to bleed it off without actually stopping. Looking away. Denying the shocks are real. Pressing the switch for the shortest possible instant. Deciding the learner is stupid and brought it on himself. And above all talking, because protest is a safety valve. The man who says this is wrong and keeps pressing has discharged his conscience and changed nothing.

Breaking out, he argues, runs a long course. Inner doubt, then doubt spoken aloud, then open dissent, then a threat to withdraw, and only then the act itself. Each step costs something, which is why so few people finish it. His large claim is that the capacity for all this is built into us because hierarchy worked, and the groups that could organise beat the groups that could not.

The line he is remembered for is this. Ordinary people, simply doing their jobs, and without any particular hostility on their part, can become agents in a terrible destructive process. He went further, and said that after watching hundreds of ordinary people submit in his own laboratory he had to conclude that Hannah Arendt's conception of the banality of evil came closer to the truth than one might dare imagine. And he refused to leave it inside the skull. The problem of obedience, he wrote, is not wholly psychological. The form and shape of society, and the division of labour that leaves each person holding only a fragment of an act, have much to do with it. The epilogue turns to the massacre at My Lai.

b: Milgram died in New York on the twentieth of December 1984, of his fifth heart attack, aged fifty one. He left his wife Alexandra, whom he had married in December 1961, and their two children.

The result travelled without him. Thomas Blass gathered the replications and found no drift over the decades, averaging around sixty one in a hundred in American studies and sixty six elsewhere. Jerry Burger built a version that stopped at a hundred and fifty volts and debriefed people immediately, and got rates close to Milgram's. A French television programme in 2010 dressed the whole thing up as a game show, and only sixteen of eighty contestants stopped before the last shock.

Then the archive answered back. In 2004 Gina Perry found hundreds of Milgram's audio tapes at Yale and spent four years tracking down surviving participants, assistants and relatives. Her account is uncomfortable, and it has to be said plainly. Around three quarters of subjects left the laboratory without being told the truth, some learning only months later by letter and some apparently never. On the tapes the experimenter does not stick to his four lines. He improvises, coaxes and argues, which means the boundary between an obedient subject and a defiant one shifts from person to person. And a good number of subjects did not believe the shocks were real. Milgram's own notes record private doubts. The famous figure is softer than the book makes it sound, and the clean script he described was not always the script in the room.

Others have reinterpreted rather than demolished. Alexander Haslam and Stephen Reicher argue that what the recordings actually show is not blind submission but engaged followership, people working hard for a cause they have been persuaded is worthwhile. James Waller pointed out how unlike genocide a laboratory is. Nobody was told the harm would be permanent, nobody knew the victim, nobody was moved by hatred, and the whole thing was over in an hour.

What survives all of it is the comparison, and the comparison is the real legacy. Move the victim nearer and obedience collapses. Let one peer refuse out loud and it very nearly vanishes. Hand a man a fragment of the job and almost all of them will finish it. You may argue about the headline number for ever. The dials are real, and most of them are in the room rather than in the man.

connects: Cialdini catalogues authority as one of six levers of compliance, where Milgram spent a decade measuring how far that single lever can be pushed.
Frankl answers from inside the camps the question Milgram set out to ask from a basement at Yale, which is what ordinary people become under a system.
Shirer watched a modern state assemble the hierarchy whose psychology Milgram later tried to rebuild one switch at a time.
note: The life is drawn from Milgram's own 1963 paper in the Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, from Obedience to Authority itself, and from standard biographical accounts including Thomas Blass's work on him. The experimental figures quoted are those Milgram published, which is why the chapter on the archive matters. Gina Perry's Behind the Shock Machine, based on tapes she found at Yale in 2004, disputes the debriefing, the consistency of the script and the belief rates, and Haslam and Reicher offer engaged followership as a rival reading. No dialogue has been invented, and the quoted lines are Milgram's published or letter wording.
recall: In Milgram's first published condition, what was the only thing the learner did before falling silent?

At three hundred volts the learner pounded on the wall of the adjoining room. After that he made no sound at all, so from then on the teacher was shocking a silence. Five of the fourteen men who broke off did so at that moment.
What were the four lines the experimenter used when a teacher wanted to stop?

In order, please continue or please go on, the experiment requires that you continue, it is absolutely essential that you continue, and you have no other choice, you must go on. A fifth line answered worries about injury by denying any permanent tissue damage.
Which single change cut obedience the most, and by how much?

Putting two other teachers in the room who refused and walked out. Obedience fell from about sixty five in a hundred to roughly one in ten, making visible peer refusal the strongest effect Milgram found.
What does Milgram mean by the agentic state?

It is the condition of seeing yourself as the instrument of someone else's purpose rather than the author of your own acts. Conscience is not lost, it is redirected to how well the task is performed, and responsibility is handed upwards.
What did Gina Perry find in the Yale tapes in 2004?

That about three quarters of subjects were never told the truth before leaving, that the experimenter improvised well beyond his four scripted lines, and that many subjects doubted the shocks were real. Her work makes the headline percentage much softer than the book suggests.
recap:
Stanley Milgram was born in the Bronx in 1933 to immigrant parents, a Hungarian baker and a Romanian mother. Relatives who had survived the camps stayed in the family flat, and at his bar mitzvah in 1946 he spoke about the Jews of Europe. He said later that he felt he should have been born into Jewish Prague in 1922 and never understood how he came to be born safe in New York. That accident set his question. Not why monsters do terrible things, but why clerks and salesmen do.

He read political science, was rejected by Harvard for knowing no psychology, talked his way in anyway, and worked as Solomon Asch's assistant. Asch had studied conformity, which is sideways pressure from equals. Milgram wanted the vertical version, where somebody with the right to ask gives an order. For his doctorate he rebuilt Asch's study using tones instead of lines, with a group that was only a tape recording, and he joked that such a group is always willing to perform at the experimenter's convenience. His gift was apparatus.

In August 1961, three months after Eichmann's trial opened, he began in a basement at Yale. Forty men, four dollars and fifty cents, a rigged draw, a grey technician's coat, and a machine with thirty switches running to four hundred and fifty volts. Twenty six of the forty went to the end, sweating and laughing nervously as they did it, while the experts had predicted that almost nobody would.

The real work was the variations. Give the victim a voice and obedience fell. Put him in the room and it halved. Make the subject hold his hand down and it halved again. Order by telephone and it collapsed, with some men quietly pressing the lowest switch while claiming otherwise. Let two peers refuse out loud and nine in ten refused too. Give a man a fragment of the job and almost all of them finished it.

The 1974 book names the mechanism. The agentic state, where conscience stops asking whether the act is right and starts asking whether it is being done well. Binding factors of sequence and politeness hold people in. Strain is bled off by looking away, blaming the victim and, most of all, by protesting while continuing. Harvard denied him tenure and he died at fifty one. Gina Perry's work in the Yale tapes later showed missing debriefs, an improvising experimenter and subjects who doubted the shocks, so treat the famous percentage gently. The comparisons are what hold.

Remember this. The dial that decides what a decent person will do is almost never inside the person. It is in the room.
stories: The forecast that was wrong by sixty

Before running anything, Milgram asked psychiatrists, students and ordinary adults to predict how far people would go. They agreed it would be almost nobody, perhaps one person in a hundred, and that anyone reaching the end of the board would be pathological. Twenty six of his forty volunteers pushed every switch to four hundred and fifty volts. The experts were not slightly out, they were wrong by a factor of sixty. The useful part is not that people obey. It is that nobody, including the professionals, can see it coming in themselves.
The men who cheated the telephone

In one variation the experimenter gave his orders by telephone from another room instead of standing behind the volunteer. Obedience collapsed to about one man in five. But the recordings and reports showed something stranger than refusal. Several men kept pressing the very lowest switch every single time while assuring the experimenter down the line that they were working through the schedule as instructed. Faced with an authority they could not see, they did not defy him. They deceived him, which tells you how expensive open disobedience feels.
Two men stand up and leave

Milgram ran a condition with three teachers, two of them actors. At a hundred and fifty volts one actor refused to continue and sat down across the room. A little later the second refused and left his chair too. The real volunteer, who had been going along like everybody else, then faced the man in the coat alone. Nine out of ten refused to finish. One visible refusal, delivered by an equal and in front of him, did what thirteen years of argument never did.
take: Before you blame a person for what happened, change one feature of the room and watch the rate move. Proximity, who gives the order and whether anyone has ever refused out loud will explain more than personality.
Conscience changes job rather than switching off
People in a hierarchy feel guilt about doing the task badly instead of about the task. If your team worries about tone and never about whether the call should happen, that is the agentic state.
Nobody agrees to four hundred and fifty volts. They agree to fifteen more than last time. Put the hard question at the start of a process, not somewhere in the middle of it.
Protest is a safety valve, not a brake
Saying this feels wrong and carrying on relieves the pressure and changes nothing. Count stops, not objections.
One visible refusal does the work of a thousand lectures
Two peers walking out took obedience from sixty five in a hundred down to one in ten. Make at least one real refusal visible in your own team, and name the person who did it.
Distance is the cheapest lever for harm
Obedience halved when the victim came into the room. Anything that keeps a decision maker away from the person affected is making harm easier, including good software.
Fragments finish jobs whole people refuse
Give someone a small subsidiary role and almost everyone goes to the end. Watch for any process where no single person can see what they are actually part of.
Check the famous studies before you quote them
The tapes show missing debriefs, an improvising experimenter and subjects who doubted the shocks. The comparisons hold up far better than the headline number, so cite those instead.
title: The Baker's Son Who Built the Shock Box
wiifm: You will come away with something more useful than the famous sixty five percent. You will know the dials Milgram actually found, the things that make a decent person carry on and the much smaller things that let them stop. You will hear how a baker's son from the Bronx turned a question about the Holocaust into a machine, what it cost him, and where the archive has since caught him out. And you will have a working test for any system you run or work inside. If stopping is socially expensive and nobody has ever done it out loud, the system is designed for obedience.
words: Acting as somebody else's instrument rather than on your own purposes.
Milgram's whole theory rests on it, the moment a volunteer stops asking whether the shock is right and starts asking whether he is reading the word pairs correctly.
To give up a responsibility or a power that was properly yours.
The teachers did not lose their judgement, they abdicated it upwards to the man in the grey coat who seemed to own the purpose.
To fix an attitude or belief in someone by patient, repeated teaching.
Milgram argues the anxiety that stops us disobeying is inculcated so early in childhood that it feels like instinct rather than training.
To clear someone, including yourself, of blame.
Deciding the learner was stupid and had brought the shocks on himself was one of the cheapest ways a subject could exculpate himself and carry on.
To make something seem or feel less serious without actually putting it right.
Protest in the Milgram room palliated the strain, which is precisely why the men who complained loudest often pressed every switch.
